newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Police beating apparently sparks Indonesian riot.
newsitem.headline: Police beating apparently sparks Indonesian riot.

text.p: An Indonesian mob, apparently incensed by a report that police had beaten a religious teacher, went on the rampage on Thursday, setting fire to churches, commercial buildings and vehicles, police and residents said.
They said the West Java town of Tasikmalaya, about 200 km southeast of Jakarta, appeared to be under siege with smoke billowing from burning buildings.
Residents contacted by telephone said police and troops had sealed off the town of about 500,000 people, but there were no immediate reports of casualties.
They said a crowd of several thousand people, many of them youths, ran amok apparently after police had beaten a religious school teacher and his two students.
"Yes, the rioting is connected to that case," a Tasikmalaya police official told Reuters. "The rioters are still going around town and we are monitoring the situation."
Another policeman earlier said three Christian churches were among the buildings set on fire. A resident said two stores were reported to be burning, while several cars had also been set afire.
In the last major riot in mainly-Moslem Indonesia, 25 churches and a temple were burnt down and five people died in October after a mob rampaged in the Situbondo area of East Java.
This riot was sparked by a court case in which a Moslem heretic subsequently received a jail term for blasphemy.
The police official in Tasikmalaya said more than 200 policemen had been deployed and reinforcements had been sought from the hilltown of Bandung, about 120 km to the northwest.
He said police were trying to determine the extent of the damage in Tasikmalaya, a key road and rail transit town from Jakarta to central Java, which produces mainly handicraft products.
A resident, Chuisan, said several churches, commercial buildings and houses had been badly damaged by groups of people, mostly youths, rampaging through the town.
"There's a group of people knocking on my door right now," he told Reuters before hanging up the telephone.
Another witness said police and soldiers had cordoned off the town. He said he could see smoke billowing from the town centre.
Political and religious analysts say Christian churches become targets for mob violence primarily for economic and social reasons, with Christians usually the more affluent members of the community.

Indonesias's Armed forces chief General Feisal Tanjung said in Irian Jaya province on Wednesday that conflicts triggered by religious differences were more dangerous than those caused by ethnic and racial differences, the official Antara news agency reported.
The trial of five Indonesians accused of taking part in the Situbondo riots opened on December 17. They were the first of 53 people expected to face trial.
More than 80 percent of Indonesia's nearly 200 million people are Moslems, but the government recognises all the world's major religions.
